title.value: The Brain-Computer Metaphor Debate Is Useless: A Matter of Semantics
title.justification: This value was chosen because it accurately reflects the main argument presented in the paper, which discusses the semantic issues surrounding the use of the brain-computer metaphor in brain sciences.
title.quote: It is commonly assumed that usage of the word 'computer' in the brain sciences reflects a metaphor. However, there is no single definition of the word 'computer' in use. In fact, based on the usage of the word 'computer' in computer science, a computer is merely some physical machinery that can in theory compute any computable function.

extractions.description: This paper examines the debate surrounding the use of the brain-computer metaphor in brain sciences. It argues that the debate is largely semantic, depending on the definition of 'computer' being used. The authors propose that the debate should be put to rest by recognizing that brains can be considered computers in the computer science sense but not in the metaphorical or lay sense, depending on context.

sustainable_development_is_central.justification: The paper focuses on theoretical and philosophical discussions in computer science and neuroscience, with no emphasis on climate or ecological sustainable development.
sustainable_development_is_central.quote: We propose that the best path forward is simply to put the debate to rest, and instead, have researchers be clear about which definition they are using in their work.

primary_category.justification: The paper does not address any topics directly relevant to climate or ecological sustainable development as its primary focus is on clarifying semantic debates within neuroscience and computer science.
primary_category.quote: The natural question that emerges from the realization that the brain-computer metaphor debate is actually just a semantic disagreement is to ask whether it matters which definition of 'computer' we adopt.

secondary_categories.justification: There are no secondary themes or discussions related to climate or ecological sustainable development within the paper.
secondary_categories.quote: We propose that the best path forward is simply to put the debate to rest, and instead, have researchers be clear about which definition they are using in their work.

primary_sub_category.justification: As the primary category is 'N/A', there is no specific sub-category relevant to climate or ecological sustainable development.
primary_sub_category.quote: In this article, we clarify these two distinct definitions. We show that if one adopts the definition from computer science, then the question is not whether computers are a good metaphor for brains, because brains arguably are literally computers based on this definition.

secondary_sub_categories.justification: With no relevant primary category/sub-category, there are no secondary sub-categories related to climate or ecological sustainable development.
secondary_sub_categories.quote: Here, we argue that closer examination of the manner in which both computer scientists and non-computer scientists use the word 'computer' indicates that there are at least two distinct definitions in operation.

applications.justification: No specific applications related to climate or ecological sustainable development are mentioned in the paper.
applications.quote: There is no single correct definition for 'computer'—but we all must be clear on what we mean when we write and speak.
